# Multiplexer

> A lightweight TCP message broker for service-to-service messaging, not a socket multiplexer and not a WebSocket server: request/reply and publish/subscribe between services on a trusted network. Peers connect over TCP, announce a peer type, and exchange typed messages routed by a declarative rules file, with round-robin load balancing, fan-out and automatic failover across active-active instances. Stateless, no single point of failure. Installs without a build on Linux x86_64: `pip install mx-multiplexer` gives the Python library and `mxcontrol`, the multiplexer itself; a release also ships `mxcontrol` as a static binary and a container image, and the C++ library as Debian and Ubuntu packages. The C++17 source builds with Bazel or make.

Vocabulary used everywhere: a peer is a client (sends requests or events) or a backend (receives requests or events, answers the requests); both talk to multiplexers. A role is what a peer does, not the class it is built on. Five classes connect a program to the multiplexers: `SyncClient` (named `Client` before 2.4.0; both names work), `ThreadedClient` and `AsyncClient` give you calls and hand you what arrives; `BaseMultiplexerServer` and `BaseThreadedMultiplexerServer`, the server classes, run a `serve_forever()` loop that calls your `handle_message()`. "Client" in a class name is part of the name, not the role: a backend is usually built on a server class, often on `ThreadedClient` or `AsyncClient`, and in a pinch on `SyncClient`. Only a peer built on `SyncClient` is passive; the other four classes run the loop all the time.

## Facts to know before reading further

- Getting it: `pip install mx-multiplexer` installs the Python package (import name `multiplexer`; the PyPI name differs because `multiplexer` there is an unrelated package) and the `mxcontrol` command that runs a multiplexer, writes rules files and generates constants: manylinux_2_28 wheels for CPython 3.10 to 3.14 on x86_64 Linux, glibc 2.28 or newer, no sdist. What these pages describe needs 2.4.0 or newer. A release also ships a static `mxcontrol` for any x86_64 Linux, the image `ghcr.io/kulewski/multiplexer:<version>` or `:latest` (distroless, nonroot, port 1980, the system rules built in; mount your rules file over /etc/mx/multiplexer.rules), and a Debian package per Debian/Ubuntu release with mxcontrol, the C++ library, headers and pkg-config (docs/packaging.md); or build from source with Bazel or make (docs/building.md). On Kubernetes: a StatefulSet behind a headless Service, one name per instance, no operator (docs/operations.md).
- Running a multiplexer: `mxcontrol run_multiplexer --address 127.0.0.1:1980 --rules multiplexer.rules` (an IP literal, an IPv6 one in brackets as in `[::1]:1980`, `[::]:1980` for every IPv6 and, on Linux, IPv4 address; 1980 is the port every page uses; `--address host:0 --port-file PATH` picks a free one); SIGTERM ends it with 0 and SIGHUP reloads the rules. Run several and give every peer all their addresses (docs/operations.md). In Docker: `docker run -d -p 1980:1980 -u "$(id -u)" -v "$PWD:/etc/mx:ro" ghcr.io/kulewski/multiplexer:latest` serves the `multiplexer.rules` of the current directory, edits put in use without a restart; on Kubernetes, a StatefulSet behind a headless Service with the rules file from a ConfigMap mounted at /etc/mx, the peers given `mx-0.mx:1980,mx-1.mx:1980,mx-2.mx:1980`, no operator (the README's "In Docker and on Kubernetes", docs/operations.md#on-kubernetes).
- Consuming it: from Python after pip, `mxcontrol generate_constants your.rules --python multiplexer_constants.py --pyi multiplexer_constants.pyi` writes the constants of your rules file, imported as `from multiplexer_constants import peers, types`; the test harness, `multiplexer.testing`, runs the package's mxcontrol, or `$MXCONTROL`. From C++, the Debian package and `g++ -std=c++17 peer.cc $(pkg-config --cflags --libs multiplexer)`, the constants written with `--cxx multiplexer/multiplexer.constants.h` on the include path before the package's copy. From Bazel, declare the repository as `@mx` with `git_repository`, call `mx_dependencies()` then `mx_setup()` in WORKSPACE, point the build at your rules file with `--@mx//:multiplexer_rules=`, depend on `@mx//multiplexer:clients` or `:servers` (Python) and `@mx//multiplexer:client` (C++); tests get `@mx//multiplexer/testing`.
- Rules files: every one starts from the system rules, which `mxcontrol generate_rules FILE` writes: the protocol's peer and message types 1 to 99 and six the libraries use by name (peer types 108 and 111, message types 112 to 115); a deployment adds its own after them, 100 and up, and generates its constants from the file (docs/rules.md).
- Semantics: a message is delivered at most once per multiplexer to whoever is connected now, nothing is queued or persisted; a request whose reply is late is sent again to another backend, so a backend may receive a request twice and every attempt has a new id; a request addressed to one instance (`to=`) reaches that instance or fails; order holds per connection, and a lane keeps a stream on one connection; no authentication, for a trusted network (docs/semantics.md).
- Addresses: a peer is given host names or addresses; a name is resolved inside the library on every attempt, each address tried in turn, so a multiplexer that moved is found at the next reconnect and a name not resolving yet is retried like a refused port, never an error.
- The rules file changes without a restart: a multiplexer reads it again every 2 s (`--rules-check-interval`) and puts a changed file in use whole once two reads in a row saw the same new bytes, so nothing half written is applied; SIGHUP and `mxcontrol rules reload` apply at once; a file that is missing, empty, without a peer type or that does not parse leaves the rules in use as they were, and `mxcontrol rules status` reports each replica's fingerprint. On Kubernetes the ConfigMap mounted as a directory updates on its own; a subPath mount or an immutable ConfigMap does not (docs/operations.md#changing-the-rules).
- Draining: a backend's `start_draining()` sends every multiplexer a `Routing` (`any`, `all`, `last_resort`; message types `PEER_CONTROL` 11 and `PEER_STATUS` 12, also carried in the welcome so a reconnect keeps it) that turns the rule-routed paths off, so requests, events and searches go to the other backends of the type at once, addressed messages still arrive, and the drain ends when every multiplexer confirmed and the work is done, `drain_seconds` at the latest; `last_resort` keeps a lone backend served, `all` kept keeps events coming; `set_routing()` on `SyncClient`, `ThreadedClient` and `AsyncClient` does the same outside a drain (docs/leaving.md).
- `is_passive` in the rules file is needed only by peer types built on `SyncClient`; ThreadedClient, AsyncClient, BaseMultiplexerServer and BaseThreadedMultiplexerServer run the loop all the time. A BaseMultiplexerServer handler must finish within the multiplexer's drop interval (90 s); BaseThreadedMultiplexerServer has no such limit.
- Building from source: Bazel 6.2.1 through Bazelisk (`.bazelversion`), a C++17 compiler (gcc 11 or newer, clang 18), `protoc` with `libprotobuf` of the same version, Python 3.10 or newer with headers and `python3-protobuf`; Asio, pybind11 and googletest are fetched by Bazel. Verified on clean Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 (docs/building.md). Without Bazel, `make` builds the same from the distribution's Asio, pybind11 (2.9 or newer) and googletest packages.

## A complete program

The README's quick start: a rules file that starts from the system rules and adds a client's and a backend's types, its constants, two multiplexers, a backend that upper-cases what it is asked and a client that asks.

```
python3 -m venv mx && . mx/bin/activate
pip install "mx-multiplexer>=2.4.0"
mxcontrol generate_rules multiplexer.rules
cat >> multiplexer.rules <<'END'
peer { type: 200 name: "WEB" }
peer { type: 201 name: "COMPUTE" }
type { type: 301 name: "COMPUTE_REQUEST" to { peer: "COMPUTE" whom: ANY } }
type { type: 302 name: "COMPUTE_RESPONSE" }
END
mxcontrol generate_constants multiplexer.rules --python multiplexer_constants.py
mxcontrol run_multiplexer --address 127.0.0.1:1980 2> mx1.log &
mxcontrol run_multiplexer --address 127.0.0.1:1981 2> mx2.log &
```

```python
# backend.py
from multiplexer.servers import BaseMultiplexerServer
from multiplexer_constants import peers, types


class Compute(BaseMultiplexerServer):
    def handle_message(self, mxmsg):
        self.send_message(message=mxmsg.message.upper(), type=types.COMPUTE_RESPONSE)


Compute([("127.0.0.1", 1980), ("127.0.0.1", 1981)], type=peers.COMPUTE).serve_forever()
```

```python
# client.py
from multiplexer.threaded_client import ThreadedClient
from multiplexer_constants import peers, types

client = ThreadedClient([("127.0.0.1", 1980), ("127.0.0.1", 1981)], type=peers.WEB)
print(client.query(b"hello", type=types.COMPUTE_REQUEST, timeout=10).message)  # b'HELLO'
client.shutdown()
```

- [Integration tests](tests/README.md)

- [The echo example](examples/echo/README.md)
- [The aio example](examples/aio/README.md): an asyncio TCP gateway in front of a chat backend, a reply to the one who asked and a broadcast to everyone; [its walkthrough](examples/aio/walkthrough.md) builds the gateway and the chat server line by line
- [The health example](examples/health/README.md): a backend on BaseMultiplexerServer whose health endpoint, on a thread of its own, answers 503 once the serve loop has not come round for a while, and its Kubernetes Deployment with the liveness probe beside the drain on a preStop hook, installed with pip; [its walkthrough](examples/health/walkthrough.md) builds it line by line, holds a handler past the limit and past the multiplexers' drop interval, and walks through its test
- [The cache example](examples/cache/README.md): a replicated cache as a Django cache backend, writes to every replica and reads from any, and a journal added by changing the rules file under the running multiplexers, installed with pip; [its walkthrough](examples/cache/walkthrough.md) builds it line by line, runs the measured steps and walks through testing a backend on the harness
- [The Channels example](examples/channels/README.md): a Django Channels channel layer on the multiplexer, group sends as events to every process and channel sends addressed to the owning process, with the tutorial's chat on it; [its walkthrough](examples/channels/walkthrough.md) builds the layer line by line, with the steps and the test
- [The inference example](examples/inference/README.md): a Django web app asking a pool of PyTorch model workers, installed with pip; [its walkthrough notebook](examples/inference/walkthrough.ipynb) builds it up step by step
- [The stream example](examples/stream/README.md): an answer that arrives token by token, as a language model's does, one request whose pieces come as follow-ups addressed to the requester and numbered and whose one reply ends it, through a pinned lane so that they arrive in order, the request sent again to the same generator when its multiplexer dies and the lost pieces asked for, a generator leaving after its answers, and the answer as Server-Sent Events from a FastAPI endpoint, installed with pip; [its walkthrough](examples/stream/walkthrough.md) builds it line by line, with the measured steps and the test
- [The audio example](examples/audio/README.md): an audio room, the browser's microphone as 10 ms frames through a Django Channels gateway to a C++ worker, each frame a query answered in a fifth of a millisecond and the result an event to everyone in the room, with a worker killed and rolled under the stream; [its walkthrough](examples/audio/walkthrough.md) builds the worker and the consumer line by line, with the measured steps and the test
